clue.text: His assignment would presumably have been the dog-watch

definitions.text: His assignment would presumably have been the dog-watch

parts.words: His assignment would presumably have been the dog-watch
parts.note: a ship's dog-watch is a short evening duty, but here it is read as the job of a dog standing guard: the three-headed hound at the gates of the classical underworld

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dog-watch' looks like naval jargon for a short shift at sea; the clue wants it read literally, a dog keeping watch, the mythical guard dog of Hades.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the three-headed hound guards the entrance to Hades, so his whole duty was a watch kept by a dog.

clue.text: Provides a crest

annotationWithheld.why: Provides a crest (6): CATERS is an anagram of A CREST, but no word signals the anagram; 'Provides' would have to be both the definition and the anagram indicator

clue.text: The imaginary — is so sweet That it enchants my sense" (Troi. & Cres.)

definitions.text: The imaginary — is so sweet That it enchants my sense

parts.words: The imaginary — is so sweet That it enchants my sense
parts.note: a gap-fill from Troilus's speech in Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida, where he anticipates the taste of love before tasting it

explanation.walkthrough: The missing word is from Troilus and Cressida, Act 3 Scene 2: Troilus imagines the flavour of love so vividly that the very thought enchants him.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun means a pleasing taste or keen enjoyment, which is what Troilus imagines savouring.

clue.text: The outcome of doing a stretch?

definitions.text: The outcome of doing a stretch?

parts.words: The outcome of doing a stretch?
parts.note: 'doing a stretch' is slang for serving a prison term, but here it is literal: pulling something longer produces added length, or more time granted

explanation.walkthrough: 'Doing a stretch' suggests jail time; the clue wants the result of stretching something, the length or time added.
explanation.definitionFit: Stretching a thing lengthens it, and the added part, or an extra period granted, is this noun.

clue.text: Could a quack beauty specialist help her?

definitions.text: Could a quack beauty specialist help her?

parts.words: Could a quack beauty specialist help her?
parts.note: 'quack' means a fraudulent practitioner, but also a duck's call: Andersen's plain cygnet, mocked among ducklings, grows into a beautiful swan

explanation.walkthrough: A quack is a fake doctor, but also what a duck says; Hans Andersen's mocked cygnet becomes beautiful without any specialist's help.
explanation.definitionFit: In Andersen's fairy tale the scorned, plain bird among the ducklings turns out to be a lovely swan, a byword for late beauty.

clue.text: Making this is child's play

parts.note: the idiom 'child's play' means something easy, but here it is literal: a toy cake of wet earth that small children make while playing

explanation.walkthrough: 'Child's play' reads as the idiom for an easy task; taken literally it is what children do in the garden with soil and water.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaping wet earth into a pretend pastry is a classic game of small children.

clue.text: These ones sound insulting

indicators.note: the word means the answer is said like the insult, when heard rather than read

parts.note: 'you nits' is an insult: a nit is a British word for a fool

explanation.surface: A complaint that certain people sound rude.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken, the answer is 'you nits'; a nit is everyday British slang for a stupid person, so the phrase is an insult.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit is a single one of something, so the plural stands for a set of ones.

clue.text: Signs that a number take refuge in harbours

indicators.note: taking refuge in a harbour means sheltering inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: harbours are ports
ten is a number

explanation.surface: Omens that several boats will shelter in harbours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A number' is a vague way to give TEN; it shelters inside PORTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Omens or warnings of what is to come are signs of the future.

clue.text: One thing the naturist doesn't fear

definitions.text: One thing the naturist doesn't fear

parts.words: One thing the naturist doesn't fear
parts.note: a nudist happily goes uncovered, so being laid bare, in the open air and to public view, holds no terror

explanation.walkthrough: The word means both being uncovered to view and being left out in the cold, neither of which troubles a nudist.
explanation.definitionFit: Being uncovered to view, or to the weather, is the state a nudist willingly embraces.

clue.text: Poe's heart

parts.note: Edgar Allan Poe wrote a famous short story about a murderer betrayed by the beating heart of his victim; its title gives the adjective for that heart

explanation.walkthrough: The heart in Poe's story keeps beating under the floorboards and gives the killer away, so it is an informer: the story's title supplies the hyphenated word.
explanation.definitionFit: Poe's story 'The Tell-Tale Heart' names its heart by this adjective, meaning one that reveals a secret.

clue.text: Mrs. Gargery's maiden name, anyway

indicators.note: read 'any way' round, forwards or backwards, the name is spelt the same, so the word tells us it reads identically in either direction

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A trivia question about a Dickens character's family name, with a shrug at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's Great Expectations Mrs Joe Gargery is Pip's older sister, so her maiden name is Pip's surname; 'anyway' is read as 'any way', since the name reads the same in both directions.
explanation.definitionFit: Mrs Gargery was born into Pip's family in Great Expectations, so her surname before marriage matches the hero's.

clue.text: Example of the pavement artist's work?

definitions.text: Example of the pavement artist's work?

parts.words: Example of the pavement artist's work?
parts.note: a pavement artist usually chalks pictures on the street, but here it is one who lays a patterned pavement of fitted tiles, a mosaic

explanation.walkthrough: A British pavement artist chalks pictures on the sidewalk for coins; read differently, the artist makes pavements of interlocking tiles.
explanation.definitionFit: A pattern of shapes fitted together with no gaps, as in mosaic flooring, is this.

clue.text: It facilitates fiddling work

parts.note: 'fiddling' suggests cheating or fidgeting, but here it is playing the fiddle: the resin rubbed on a violin bow so it grips the strings

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiddling work' sounds like fraud or fussy handiwork; it means violin playing, which needs resin on the bow hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Violinists rub this hardened pine resin on the bow so that the hair grips the strings and sounds them.

clue.text: Hall Caine wrote of one of these

definitions.text: Hall Caine wrote of one of these

parts.words: Hall Caine wrote of one of these
parts.note: the novelist Hall Caine wrote a best-selling 1887 novel titled after a judge of the Isle of Man, a post of which there are two

explanation.walkthrough: Hall Caine's novel 'The Deemster' is about one of the two judges of the Isle of Man; the clue asks for the plural.
explanation.definitionFit: On the Isle of Man the senior judges carry this old title, and Caine's novel takes one as its subject.

clue.text: Voices stir me strangely-is it the measure of their liquid qualities ?

definitions.text: the measure of their liquid qualities

indicators.note: the words before it are arranged strangely, that is, put in an odd new order to form the instrument

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether the oddly stirring voices they hear are being judged on how smoothly they flow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strangely' rearranges the twelve letters of VOICES STIR ME; 'is it' links them to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This instrument gauges viscosity, how thick or runny a fluid is, which is a liquid's key quality.

clue.text: "How sweet the sleeps upon this bank " (Mer, of Venice)

definitions.text: How sweet the sleeps upon this bank

parts.words: How sweet the sleeps upon this bank
parts.note: a gap-fill from Lorenzo's speech to Jessica in Act 5 of The Merchant of Venice, describing night light resting on a grassy bank

explanation.walkthrough: The page prints a dash where the missing word goes; the line is Lorenzo's in Act 5 of The Merchant of Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: Lorenzo pictures the gentle glow from the night sky lying on the bank like a sleeper.

clue.text: With which the Persian warrior took a short cut to victory ?

definitions.text: With which the Persian warrior took a short cut to victory ?

parts.words: With which the Persian warrior took a short cut to victory ?
parts.note: 'short cut' suggests a quicker route, but a curved oriental sword gives a cut with a short blade swing

explanation.walkthrough: 'Took a short cut' looks like taking a quicker path; the warrior's cut is a slash with his curved sword.
explanation.definitionFit: This curved, single-edged sabre was the classic weapon of Persian and Turkish fighters.

clue.text: Resounding designer ?

definitions.meaning: loud and reverberating, like a mournful bell
read as two words, a man who plans

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition splits the answer into PLAN and GENT, a gentleman who draws up plans, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Deep, mournful and reverberating sounds are described by this word; split, it is also a planning gentleman.

clue.text: His loot was worth much more than five shillings

definitions.text: His loot was worth much more than five shillings

parts.words: His loot was worth much more than five shillings
parts.note: a crown was the old British coin worth five shillings; the thief meant here stole the Crown Jewels from the Tower of London in 1671

explanation.walkthrough: A crown was an old British coin worth five shillings; Colonel Thomas Blood tried to steal the Crown Jewels in 1671, a haul worth far more than the coin.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish adventurer Thomas Blood, who held a colonel's rank, seized the regalia from the Tower of London.

clue.text: Peterkin's find was large and round as well as this

definitions.text: Peterkin's find was large and round as well as this

parts.words: Peterkin's find was large and round as well as this
parts.note: in Southey's poem 'After Blenheim' little Peterkin finds a skull 'so large, and ..., and round' by the stream

explanation.walkthrough: Robert Southey's poem 'After Blenheim' has the child Peterkin bring in a skull found by the rivulet, 'that was so large, and smooth, and round'.
explanation.definitionFit: The skull Peterkin found was even and free of roughness, the third adjective in Southey's line.

clue.text: Sacred flower of India ?

parts.note: 'flower' reads as a bloom such as the lotus, but here it is something that flows: a holy river of India

explanation.walkthrough: In crosswords a 'flower' is often a river (a thing that flows); India's holiest river is meant, not the lotus.
explanation.definitionFit: Hindus revere this great river of northern India as a goddess.

clue.text: One subject to such madness

parts.note: read as 'madness restricted to one subject': an obsession with a single idea, the Greek for 'one' joined to the word for frenzy

explanation.walkthrough: 'One subject to' looks like a person who suffers madness; it means a madness confined to one subject, which is exactly what the word's Greek parts say.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the term for an obsessive fixation on a single idea while sane in other respects.

clue.text: Despite black looks, she gave a lift to those in trouble

definitions.text: Despite black looks, she gave a lift to those in trouble

parts.words: Despite black looks, she gave a lift to those in trouble
parts.note: a 'Black ...' is slang for a police van, which gives arrested people, those in trouble with the law, a ride

explanation.walkthrough: 'Black Maria' is old British and American slang for a police van; it carries people in trouble with the law, and 'black looks' is its colour.
explanation.definitionFit: The woman's name completes the slang term for a police van, which ferries the arrested.

clue.text: At fifty Lady Hamilton makes a proposition

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty
Emma, Lady Hamilton, was Nelson's mistress

explanation.surface: Nelson's mistress, at fifty, propositions someone.
explanation.walkthrough: Emma Hamilton was Admiral Nelson's lover; 'makes' links the wordplay to the definition, which is the logician's sense of 'proposition', not an advance.
explanation.definitionFit: In logic and mathematics a subsidiary statement proved on the way to a theorem is this.

clue.text: He is taken into the party, but not in a practical sense

indicators.note: taken into describes one piece being admitted inside the other, like a recruit joining the party

parts.note: the Tory party is Britain's Conservative party
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man joins a political party, though without doing anything useful there.
explanation.walkthrough: Tory is the familiar name for Britain's Conservative party. The definition plays on 'in practice' against its opposite: thought rather than action.
explanation.definitionFit: Something true only in principle, as opposed to practice, holds as an abstract idea rather than in real operation.

clue.text: Sound as a bell

parts.note: the idiom 'sound as a bell' means in perfect health, but 'sound' is the noun here: the noise a ringing bell makes

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase looks like the idiom for being perfectly fit; it really asks for the noise a bell makes.
explanation.definitionFit: The two-note chime of a swinging church bell is represented by this rhyming imitative phrase.

clue.text: The spiritualist takes it to heart

definitions.text: The spiritualist takes it to heart

indicators.note: the word spiritualist holds this one at its centre, in its heart, with letters either side

explanation.surface: A medium takes some rite very seriously.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits in the middle of 'spiritualist', between SPI and IST; and a spiritualist's séance is itself a ceremony, so the whole clue defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A set ceremonial procedure, such as a séance, is the kind of rite a spiritualist observes.

clue.text: Quickly gets a grasp of music

explanation.surface: Someone picks up a working knowledge of music in no time.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as learning music fast; it splits into a verb for grabbing and a noun for brief bits of melody.
explanation.definitionFit: To grab quickly is to seize, and brief fragments of a tune are heard in short bursts; one word covers both.
